anchor.quote: Adjectives
Adjectives describe, compare and define nouns and words that act as nouns. Use adjectives to help people understand meaning.

not_rules.note: Introductory educational explanation and broad advice.

anchor.quote: Adjectives describe nouns
Adjectives describe nouns, noun phrases and noun clauses.
Adjectives usually go immediately before the noun. They can go elsewhere in a sentence – for example, as a predicate.
Adjectives also modify noun phrases and noun clauses.
Different types of words, such as nouns, can also function as adjectives.
Adjectives can affect clarity

not_rules.note: Candidate heading functioning as section title.

anchor.quote: Because adjectives are modifiers, they can affect clarity. A lack of clarity can cause users to lose trust in government content.

anchor.quote: Most adjectives use different degrees for comparisons

not_rules.note: Descriptive section header on degrees of adjectives.

anchor.quote: Degree shows the relative scale of the words being described, such as speed, size or quality. Most adjectives can have ‘degree’.
These adjectives usually follow the pattern of adding ‘-er’ or ‘-est’ to the end to show the degree.
Not all adjectives follow the regular pattern of ‘fast–faster–fastest’. These irregular adjectives have different patterns.
Some adjectives don’t have a different form to show degree. They show degree by using ‘more’ for comparative or ‘most’ for superlative.
Some adjectives don’t have degree because you can’t compare them. For example, nothing can be more unique than something else.

rules.quote: A compound adjective usually has a hyphen if the adjective is before the noun it is describing.
rules.violation_condition: a compound adjective placed before the noun it modifies that is written without hyphens
when: The compound adjective appears before the noun it is describing.
Does not apply when the compound adjective appears after the noun (e.g. as a predicate).

covers.quote: Write strings of adjectives in an order that creates a more natural-sounding English.
evaluative – features of a noun that you can measure or compare
descriptive – features of a noun that you can’t measure
definitive – features of a noun that are intrinsic to the noun.

examples.note: Ordered: beautiful (evaluative), round (descriptive), committee (definitive).

parts.quote: A beautiful round committee table

rules.specification: Adjectives in a string modifying a single noun should follow the order: 1. evaluative, 2. descriptive, 3. definitive.
rules.violation_condition: a string of adjectives modifying a noun that violates the order of evaluative, descriptive, and definitive
rules.why: G-1, G-4: Rule governing order in strings of adjectives, folding the list items defining categories into the rule.

covers.quote: commas between adjectives of the same type
no commas between adjectives of different types
no commas and no ‘and’ before definitive adjectives.
You can also use ‘and’ instead of commas to help the sentence flow more smoothly.

examples.note: Comma between descriptive adjectives 'large' and 'black'; no comma before definitive 'nuclear'.

parts.quote: A large, black nuclear submarine

examples.note: Comma between descriptive adjectives 'new' and 'red'; no commas before definitive adjectives.

parts.quote: A new, red long-range electric car

examples.note: Using 'and' instead of commas between descriptive adjectives.

parts.quote: A new and shiny red long-range electric car

rules.specification: Place commas between adjectives of the same type. Do not place commas between adjectives of different types. Do not use commas or 'and' before definitive adjectives.
rules.violation_condition: missing commas between adjectives of the same type in a string, or unwanted commas between adjectives of different types, or a comma or 'and' before a definitive adjective
when: You can also use 'and' instead of commas between adjectives of the same type to help sentence flow.
